data.title: Chamberlain appeased Hitler — Zelensky will not and should not appease Putin
data.description:
History, they say, doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes. Right now, history is much closer to repeating itself.

Or at least, that appears to be the case regarding administration emissary Steve Witkoff’s endless courtship of Russian president Vladimir Putin. As a former senior White House official in the George H.W. Bush administration put it to me this week, “Witkoff says he trusts Putin. It’s the same thing that Neville Chamberlain said about [Adolf] Hitler.”

Actually, Witkoff has gone further than Chamberlain ever did. The American negotiator praised the Russian mass-murderer as “a humanitarian.” Chamberlain never said anything of the sort — he detested Hitler.

In September 1938, two weeks before he capitulated and signed the Munich agreement allowing Hitler to dismember Czechoslovakia and seize the Sudetenland, the British Prime Minister told his cabinet that Hitler was “a gangster” and added that the Nazi dictator was “the commonest little dog I have ever seen.’” If that were not enough, Chamberlain also described him as “entirely undistinguished. You would never notice him in a crowd and would take him for the house painter he once was.”

Hitler had as little respect for Chamberlain as Putin likely has for Witkoff. The boorish Nazi was not as polite about his counterpart, calling him “the old a——.” In public, Putin has told Witkoff and his fellow negotiator Jared Kushner, “We are comfortable working with you.” That does not necessarily indicate what he thinks of them in private.

It is worth recalling that in his effort to seize the Sudetenland, Hitler turned on the charm, and it certainly swayed the British prime minister. As Chamberlain wrote to his sister: “various people who were with Hitler after my interview [said] that he had been very favorably impressed. … In short I had established a certain confidence, which was my aim, and in spite of the hardness and ruthlessness I thought I saw in his face I got the impression that here was a man who could be relied upon when he had given his word.”

Thinking that he could rely on Hitler’s word did not mean that Chamberlain changed his view of the Nazi’s character, however. He bore no illusions about Hitler being anything other than a thug and certainly not a humanitarian.

In claiming the Sudetenland, Hitler employed the same arguments that Putin would conjure up nearly a century later. Hitler asserted that all he wanted was that part of Czechoslovakia whose population was 50 percent German. He also frequently stated that he sought peace but at the same time wanted to rectify the European security balance, which the Versailles Treaty has rendered unfavorable to Germany.

Putin has argued that Russia must incorporate Ukraine’s four oblasts with Russian-speaking majorities. And, like Hitler, he wishes to reconstruct Europe’s security architecture. He seeks to roll back NATO’s post-1997 expansion, or, at a minimum, ensure that NATO does not station any troops in those states that joined the alliance after that date.

In pandering to Putin, and in laying down a framework for a deal that Zelensky might be expected to accept, Witkoff is effectively echoing Chamberlain’s assessment of the Sudetenland crisis as “a quarrel in a faraway country, between people of whom we know nothing.”

Chamberlain felt that Czechoslovakia, a country created after World War I, simply was not worth fighting for or even supporting. Evidently, the American negotiators share a similar view of Ukraine, a country created as the Cold War ended.

The Czechs were actually militarily powerful. Had they received British and French support, they might well have withstood a German assault, if the Nazis had chosen to attack — which they might not have. Nevertheless, Eduard Benes, the Czech president, recognized that neither of the two major European powers was prepared to support him. He felt that he had no choice but to capitulate to Hitler’s demands.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has a different disposition and faces a different situation. Over five years, he has fought the Russians to a standstill while benefitting from intermittent American support and increasing European assistance. Unlike Benes, he is in no mood to capitulate.

Washington reportedly is pressing Zelensky to reach an agreement to terminate the war by year’s end. To do so, he would have to cede four oblasts to Moscow and possibly four others. Zelensky has no incentive to capitulate to Putin; time could be on his side. Whereas Chamberlain told his Cabinet that “Herr Hitler was telling the truth,” Zelensky has no such illusions about Putin. Instead, he knows that in just weeks the Democrats will control Congress and afford him far more support than he is currently receiving. He is unlikely to cave to the Russians; nor should he.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Democrats, forget the Voting Rights Act: Fix Rucho
data.description:
The left has been apoplectic about the gutting of the Voting Rights Act by the conservative majority on the U.S. Supreme Court.

The final nail in the coffin was Louisiana v. Callais this past term, which held that a violation of the Voting Rights Act requires intentional racial discrimination and further prohibited the intentional creation of Black congressional districts without such a showing. The court also observed that gerrymanders with political motivations are not necessarily racially discriminatory, even if they negatively affect Black voters. 

But this justifiable concern with the Voting Rights Act is obscuring a greater immediate threat. What really undermines Black political representation in America is not Callais, but a 2019 case on a different subject: Rucho v. Common Cause, which held that political gerrymanders cannot be challenged in federal court no matter how extreme. Partisan gerrymanders were held by the court to be political questions. Rucho, not Callais, is why Black political representation is disappearing in some states. 

To understand the interplay of Callais and Rucho, one need only look at what happened in Tennessee. Memphis used to have an urban core of Black voters in one compact congressional district next to a large, white-dominated suburban and rural district. That older map, adopted in 2022, reflected the normal pattern of legislative districting based on how Americans tend to group themselves.

Once Callais was decided, however, the Tennessee state legislature removed the longstanding ban on mid-decade congressional redistricting and carved Memphis up into three sprawling congressional districts, two of which extended all the way to Nashville, 200 miles away.

The resulting congressional map pays no attention to traditional districting norms, such as compactness and preservation of political boundaries. It looks more like a plate of spaghetti than a congressional district map. The result was three white districts and no Black district. 

All this was clearly intentional. You would think that it obviously violates Callais’s ban on intentional racial discrimination. But it probably does not, because of Callais’s strong suggestion that political gerrymanders are not necessarily racially discriminatory even when Black voters lose out.

The Republicans in the Tennessee legislature freely admitted that they were redistricting to eliminate a likely Democratic congressional district in Memphis. Hence, this was a political, not a racial, gerrymander. Black voters were just collateral damage. Under Callais, this is not a violation of the Voting Rights Act.

Forget that this reasoning is absurd, as if political partisans could not also be racist. The point is that Congress can act to undo what happened to Memphis.

Congress cannot directly reverse Callais. The Supreme Court was interpreting the Voting Rights Act against a background of equal protection principles. If Congress tried to weaken the intentional discrimination standard, the conservative majority on the court would very likely find the effort unconstitutional.

What Congress can do is reverse Rucho. In that case, the court held that political gerrymanders represent a political question because it is not obvious what a fair legislative map looks like. There was no judicially manageable standard. 

But a judicial judgment like that is subject to change by Congress, which has wide discretion to enforce voting standards for congressional elections. All Congress has to do is ban congressional maps in which partisan considerations substantially predominate over traditional districting norms. Congress could even go further and prohibit mid-decade redistricting and weirdly shaped maps altogether. 

With these changes, Tennessee’s treatment of Memphis would be plainly illegal. Memphis would very likely be restored to its simple, compact congressional district. 

Admittedly, a federal statute like that would not really increase Black representation. It would only outlaw the worst Republican excesses. Many people would like to see a more aggressive challenge to the court’s voting rights interpretations.  

That fight, however, is not likely to be successful, at least in the short run. For now, Congress should act to keep Republicans from eliminating Black representation everywhere they have a state legislative majority. A simple federal statute outlawing excessive political gerrymanders would do that without the likelihood of a prolonged legal challenge.    

Democrats overcame a lot of the Republican gerrymandering in the 2026 midterm elections But even with the blue tsunami, the Republican gerrymander of Memphis worked. Three white Republicans were elected. And in future elections, the existing Republican gerrymanders are going to be more effective than they were in 2026, with its lopsided Democratic majorities. 

If Democrats want to retain control of the House in the future, overturning Rucho is absolutely necessary. And, fortunately, it would not be hard to do.  

Returning the Voting Rights Act to its rightful place as promoting an increase in Black political participation is a worthy goal. But that goal cannot become an excuse for not acting to protect Black voters immediately. Democrats should forget about the Voting Rights Act for now and overturn Rucho first. 

Bruce Ledewitz is a professor of law emeritus at the Thomas R. Kline School of Law of Duquesne University. He is the author of the forthcoming book, “The Last Master of the Tradition: Charles Black and the Future of Constitutional Democracy.”

data.title: What would net-zero by 2050 cost, and what would it buy? We have the numbers.
data.description:
Earlier this week, the United Nations Climate Summit in Turkey, collapsed without a final agreement after two days of overtime. More than 130 countries as well as a large number of U.S. states have pledged to reach net zero, most by 2050. Yet through two weeks of talks, the most basic question went unasked: what would net zero by 2050 cost, and how much good would it do? That is odd, because the UN already owns the tools to find out.

So I built NetZeroCostBenefit.com, a website that lets anyone see what the U.S., or any other country or group of countries, would achieve by reaching net zero in 2050, what it would cost, and what the climate benefit would be worth.

None of the inputs are mine: The climate model it employs, known by the acronym MAGICC, is used throughout the U.N.’s own climate reports and can translate any country’s promised emissions cuts into lower temperatures by the year 2100. The costs come from U.N. surveys of economic models, and the damage estimates come from the two most recent syntheses of the economics of warming.

Anyone can check the arithmetic. For its latest report and updates, the climate panel gathered nearly a thousand model estimates of what climate policy costs. Almost none of them get anywhere near to net-zero by 2050, because it is so hard and costly.

Only three models reach net zero starting from today’s actual emissions, rather than assuming cuts that began years ago. They find that global net-zero would cost between 3 percent and 19 percent of global GDP in 2050. That’s because expensive energy throttles growth.

My website uses the middle estimate, of a loss of 7.2 percent of GDP in 2050 against current policies.

The estimation of benefits comes from the two most recent syntheses of the damage from warming — one by one of the most quoted climate economists, Richard Tol, and the other by William Nordhaus, the only climate economist to win the Nobel Prize in economics. Given the warming the U.N. model projects under current policies, climate change will cost the world 1.8 percent to 2.8 percent of its GDP by 2100. That is a real loss, but nowhere near the catastrophes bandied about. It is also a lot less than a 7.2 percent loss of GDP, and a lot further away.

But then there’s the other side of the equation. Net-zero only avoids part of the climate damage projected. Nor does any single country’s effort buy much. If the U.S. reaches net zero by 2050 and stays there while the rest of the world keeps its current policies, the model projects global temperatures in 2100 would be only 0.14 degrees Fahrenheit lower. So nobody would notice the difference in temperature, but Americans would certainly notice the added costs.

In 2045 alone, the model puts the cost at $1.2 trillion. From 2027 to 2100, the cost adds up to $12.7 trillion in today’s money. The global climate benefit adds up to just under $2 trillion. The American sacrifice delivers 15 cents of benefits for every dollar spent.

Some will object that no country should look at its own numbers this way, because if everyone notices large costs but tiny benefits, nothing will get done. But the math doesn’t improve with pooling. As the website shows, each nation ends up doing much less good for the world than what it puts in by adopting the net-zero goal.

Indeed, when you look at the whole world, global net zero by 2050 would avoid $24 trillion in climate damage this century but cost $255 trillion — both in today’s dollars. So that’s nine cents on the dollar.

The problem isn’t that countries act alone. It is that the policy itself costs far more than it delivers.

Fossil fuels remain cheap and plentiful, despite price fluctuations. It is little wonder that they still supply more than four-fifths of global energy, or that emissions rose again last year. At the pace of the last half-century, they won’t be gone by 2050 — they will be gone a millennium later, in 2997.

None of this means that climate change is harmless. It is indeed a real challenge, and the smart fix is to invest more in green-energy research and development, so that clean energy eventually outcompetes fossil fuels and becomes cheaper for everyone. Instead, many politicians continue to insist on expensive, inefficient policies, as if industrial economies could run on sunshine and good intentions.

Net-zero by 2050 is an egregiously bad deal. Across 31 climate summits, delegates have ignored this reality. Now, anyone can run the numbers.

Bjorn Lomborg is President of the Copenhagen Consensus, Visiting Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, and author of “False Alarm” and “Best Things First.”

data.title: Hackers break into US Air Force cloud computing platform: Report
data.description:
Hackers breached the Air Force’s main cloud computing platform in recent weeks, risking sensitive data, according to a new report from Reuters, the latest in a string of cyber incidents and outages at government agencies.

Reuters reported Friday that according to three sources, hackers broke into the Air Force’s Cloud One platform, which hosts sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

Two of the sources told Reuters the hack had been found in the past month or so, as the system was being upgraded. Reuters reported that it had not uncovered who the hackers are, how far they had gotten into the system and if data was swiped from Cloud One.

The reported hack follows other breaches in recent days.

The CIA said Tuesday that some unclassified of its systems were exposed in a hack. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said its systems were also impacted by the breach.

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, said Thursday it’s investigating an intrusion into some online systems.

Federal agencies have also been hit by outages that spurred widespread fears of malicious activity.

Last week, the National Security Agency faced a network outage, disrupting a classified internal network.

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop earlier this month, lasting for over four hours. Authorities pointed to a router in Arkansas and a Texas-based radar site as the two probable reasons behind the outage.

On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said that Americans should get ready for upgrades to aging infrastructure and multiple systems. He advised that there would be “bumps in the road” in the wake of the recent tech failures.

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems,” he told CNN’s Dana Bash. “They should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”

The Hill has reached out to the Pentagon about the reported Cloud One breach.

data.title: It's up to Congress to clean up the country's prediction-market mess
data.description:
In the space of just eight days last month, the fight over sports “prediction markets” stopped being a regulatory dispute and became something closer to a constitutional standoff. 

On Oct. 20, Utah sued Kalshi and two Susquehanna market-making firms in state court, alleging that Kalshi’s sports contracts constitute illegal gambling. On Oct. 26, the U.S. and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission sued Utah in federal court — the 10th state the agency has taken on.

Two days later, Utah’s attorney general filed criminal charges against KalshiEX and its two co-founders, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara: 12 felony counts of online gambling promotion, a second-degree felony count of pattern of unlawful activity and a misdemeanor, built on wagers an undercover agent placed on football and other games. 

“Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said. Kalshi called the charges “a crazy overreach.” Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig said that Congress made his agency “the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets.” 

Each side says Congress has already decided. The trouble is that the law they are fighting over, the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, was written years before anyone was trading NFL spreads on a federally registered exchange.

Congress must stop letting prosecutors and appeals courts guess what it meant and instead state its own clear meaning. 

The courts cannot agree. In April, a divided Third Circuit panel sided with Kalshi against New Jersey. In August, the Ninth Circuit ruled for Nevada. A federal judge in Utah ruled in August that the state’s gambling laws apply, and the Tenth Circuit refused to pause that ruling. Yet in Arizona, a federal judge blocked the state’s criminal case against Kalshi at the feds’ request. On Nov. 3, the Second Circuit declined to shield Kalshi and Coinbase from New York and Connecticut while their appeals continue. AskSpinner News tracks this litigation, and the map keeps getting more crowded, not less.

New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to take on the question, in Flaherty v. KalshiEX; Kalshi’s response is due Dec. 7. Ohio and 38 other states, plus the District of Columbia, have filed in support of New Jersey. So have former Sen. Christopher Dodd (D-Conn.), one of the law’s namesakes, and former Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Gary Gensler.

When the people who wrote and implemented a statute are filing amicus briefs about what it means, the statute is no longer doing its job. 

Even a Supreme Court ruling would settle less than it seems. The justices can tell us whether Dodd-Frank preempts state gambling law, but they cannot write the rules a sports-betting market needs. Today the answer to basic consumer-protection questions depends on which label wins.

Most states bar sports betting under 21; Kalshi accepts users from 18, a gap the American Gaming Association highlighted in its Supreme Court brief, citing a CNN estimate that 18- to 20-year-olds had traded about $5.4 billion on the platform by late August. Self-exclusion lists, advertising limits and problem-gambling funding are all built around state licenses. A preemption ruling either sweeps those away for one class of company or strands a federally registered industry in 50 different legal regimes. 

Congress can fix this with a short bill. It should decide, explicitly, whether contracts on the outcome of sporting events listed on registered exchanges are swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act. 

If Congress says no, it should give exchanges a defined wind-down period, so that the transition happens on a timetable rather than through criminal summonses issued to executives. 

If Congress says yes, it should attach a federal floor that matches what bettors get from state regulators: a minimum age of 21 for sports contracts, participation in state self-exclusion lists, advertising standards and a funding stream for problem-gambling services. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission was built to police manipulation and counterparty risk, not gambling harm, and it should not have to improvise those rules. 

Either answer is defensible. What is not defensible is the current approach: a federal agency suing 10 states, a state charging company founders with felonies over conduct a federal regulator calls lawful, and customers whose protections depend on their ZIP code.  

A federal judge in Salt Lake City heard the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s emergency motion against Utah on Nov. 20 without ruling from the bench. Congress does not need to wait for a court ruling, or for the Supreme Court, to do its job.

Kimi Yu is the founder and CEO of AskSpinner, a global gambling industry platform covering industry insight and regulatory developments.

data.title: The 2028 presidential election cycle is all about Trump
data.description:
Ever since Donald Trump descended Trump Tower’s golden escalator on June 16, 2015, to announce his presidential intentions, he has dominated the political universe. Eleven years later, as a term-limited, lame-duck president, loath to relinquish power and addicted to media attention, he will try to make the race to succeed him all about him.

Therefore, the 2028 presidential election cycle, President Trump’s last chance to wield power by selecting an heir to cement his legacy, is poised to be uniquely dramatic and unpredictable. No one could have predicted the 2024 presidential election’s out-of-bounds events — Trump’s near-assassination and President Biden’s last-minute withdrawal. So what sort of what-ifs can we reasonably discuss?

What if, by Election Day 2028, Trump is not the incumbent. This is a touchy topic but not a terribly unlikely one. Trump turns 82 in June 2028. Many people pass away at that age. Also, a severe mental or physical health crisis could trigger the 25th Amendment if Trump is “unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office.” That determination rests with Vice President JD Vance and a majority of Trump’s Cabinet, who would have to initiate removal by submitting a written declaration to Congress. Team Trump likely agrees that Trump’s disappearance from the political scene would improve Republicans’ chances of retaining the White House.

With Democrats soon to control the House and Senate, impeachment is possible and conviction unlikely. But Senate Republicans’ fear of losing in 2028 might change that assumption.

So what happens if Vice President JD Vance becomes president? Assuming he then runs for a full term; how would Vance lead the post-Trump era? Would he denigrate or defend the administration in which he played a starring role? Moreover, if necessary, would Vance pardon Trump, as President Gerald Ford pardoned President Richard Nixon, and risk losing his own election in the process?

Speculation aside, Vance is likely to retain his current title. The question of whether he will run for president without Trump’s endorsement will answered by spring 2027. I suspect that if Trump does not endorse him, Vance will announce that he will not run, and he will save face by citing family concerns. Trump could deflect, saying, “Let the people decide.” He may believe that anyone he endorses would lose the general election because they aren’t him.

Yet if Trump does endorse his likely heir, watch Vance turn himself into a political pretzel, defending Trump to win his “third term” as the president hovers over and monitors his campaign.

Meanwhile, Marco Rubio, secretary of State and national security advisor, is backstage, waiting for the Vance-Trump decision to be resolved. He has long dreamed of becoming the first Hispanic president (see his 2016 campaign), but he now carries Trump’s baggage. Will Rubio resign in 2027 to pursue his destiny? Would he “go rogue” and tell the world what he really thinks of Trump, as he did in 2016? If Vance bows out, would Trump endorse Rubio, who would then launch his campaign? What would Trump demand in return for an endorsement? Would Rubio even want Trump’s endorsement?

The latter question is relevant after Trump’s controversial Nov. 20 press conference, during which he said, “I can’t speak to America,” and rambled for nearly 90 minutes. Vance and Rubio stood behind the president like wooden puppets, even as Trump (jokingly) denigrated them as potential successors in favor of Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff. Miller’s performance at the podium, with countless lies and exaggerations was music to Trump’s ears.

For now, Vance and Rubio are caught in Trump’s magnetic political force-field, negatively supercharged since the midterms, resulting in a new tight race among Republican primary voters. RealClearPolitics polling averages show Rubio at 35.4 percent support to Vance’s 34 percent.

Furthermore, until the Trump-Rubio-Vance dance is done, less popular Republican presidential primary wannabes — such as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and soon-to-be former Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis — can only make noise.

Turning to the crowded Democratic field, the RealClear polling averages are meaningless this early, before debates start in June. Still, the big news is that Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) has leapt into second place with 15 percent support and is the man to watch.

Ossoff nips at the heels of first-place former Vice President Harris, who has 16.5 percent support. But the losing 2024 presidential nominee is only treading water with name recognition while debating whether to run again.

Summarizing the 2028 race, Trump, the showman, is the opening and closing act. The unpopular yet powerful lame-duck president is declining but remains the daily wild card. By design, he will dominate the next two chaotic years with jaw-dropping headlines, endless wars, bold lies and exaggerations, while shirking responsibility when things go wrong.

As always — just the way he likes it—Trump is a force of nature shaping the political climate, forcing every candidate to react to him.

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008.

data.title: Lutnick in the hot seat as senators vow to crack down on AI chip leaks to China
data.description:
Senators in both parties say that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is in the hot seat in the wake of revelations that Nvidia sold billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech chips to a Singapore-based company whose former senior executive, Alice Huang, is accused of being a Chinese spy.

Lawmakers in both parties criticized President Trump’s intervention to persuade Nvidia’s board to bring Jensen Huang back as its CEO after he admitted to the extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom American intelligence said had contact with a Chinese spy agency.

But while senators have limited ability to change Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang, they can exert more pressure on Lutnick, whose department depends on appropriations from Congress.

“I think that Mr. Lutnick’s got a host of problems,” said Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the incoming chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee who also sits on the Senate Banking Committee, which will hear testimony from Huang next week.

Warner suggested the Commerce Department may have allowed Nvidia to make sensitive technology sales to companies in addition to Megaspeed, the company connected to Alice Huang, that undermined restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips. 

“The idea that the Commerce Department has been allowing potentially not just some of these one-off descriptions of [chip sales] that Nvidia’s been doing but through other Chinese shell companies — we deserve answers,” he said.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the current chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said he had warned the Trump administration that advanced chips were getting past export controls and called on Congress to pass legislation to tighten restrictions.

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other,” Cotton posted on the social platform X.

Lutnick is coming under heavy scrutiny from both Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill after media outlets reported that he resisted pressure from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to put Megaspeed, the company previously affiliated with Alice Huang, on a trade blacklist.

Bessent confronted Lutnick earlier this month over why the Commerce Department had not banned the sale of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed, according to The New York Times.

Bessent told CNBC in an interview that he was frustrated over the delay in restricting chip sales and blamed the Commerce Department for not acting.

“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said, adding that the Commerce Department “has the pen” and suggesting that it should explain “their internal processes.”

Democrats, who will control the Senate and House in January, are pressing for answers about whether Lutnick may have been motivated by a financial conflict of interest.

They want to know whether data centers in Southeast Asian countries that supplied advanced computing power to China had financial ties to Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm that Lutnick once led and is now run by his sons.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee, said Lutnick and other members of the Trump administration may “have converging personal, political, corporate and financial interests in making sure” Jensen Huang remains as Nvidia’s CEO.

Lawmakers want to know what role Lutnick may have played in delaying the implementation of rules to restrict the sale of chips to companies such as Megaspeed and A201, a data center based in Malaysia, that allegedly provided China access to advanced computing power.

The Commerce Department has said Lutnick has complied with all ethics rules.

But key Republicans have joined Democrats in calling on Lutnick to testify about his role overseeing policies and regulations on chip exports.

Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has asked Lutnick to appear before his panel next month to answer questions.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the Commerce Department appeared to “knowingly” allow sensitive AI technology to skirt export restrictions.

“It appears that they knowingly allowed this to happen. Scott Bessent has been saying, ‘Stop it.’ So I want to get both of them in front of a committee, put them under oath,” he said on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“If Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” he added.

This has prompted speculation on Capitol Hill that Lutnick’s future leadership of the Commerce Department could be on shaky ground.

Lutnick will have to answer tough questions about a new report in The Atlantic that he transferred federal agents who were tasked with investigating the smuggling of advanced AI chips to his personal security detail, taking those agents off a critical national security job.

Incoming Senate Commerce Committee Chair Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said she has “great concerns about his leadership of Commerce.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said Lutnick should resign amid reports that the Commerce Department slow-walked export controls for AI chips.

Tillis said Lutnick was briefed on the findings by U.S. intelligence agencies that Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy before Trump invited the Nvidia CEO to join him on Air Force One in Alaska en route to a trip to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He said Lutnick should have intervened to block Huang from joining the president, something that Rubio tried to do.

“It was my understanding that Lutnick had been briefed on it too. Let’s just say for the sake of argument that the president was distracted and did not remember telling him about it. Lutnick should have damn well should have known,” Tillis said.

He said it was not appropriate for Huang to join Trump on the high-level trip. He also cited what he called Lutnick’s “entanglements with investments in Nvidia.”

Asked if Lutnick should resign, Tillis said: “I think he should roll.”

The Hill reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.

data.title: Zelensky on Trump calling Putin 'friend': 'Same as somebody saying about Hitler' in WWII
data.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said President Trump calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a “friend” was the “same as somebody saying about Hitler” in World War II. 

When asked during a BBC interview how he felt about Trump’s comment about Putin, Zelensky stated “it’s up to the President of the United States, but it’s strange.”

Putin was “an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend, a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody say about Hitler during the Second World War that he is a good friend. No, he is not a friend,” Zelensky continued. 

Trump called Putin his “friend” right before the pair walked into a room with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The president has enjoyed an amicable relationship with his Russian counterpart, especially with recent trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China.

Trump signaled previously that he wanted the Russian-Ukraine war to end, as the conflict will reach the five-year mark in February.

In his BBC interview, Zelensky expressed he felt there needed to be “more progress” in U.S.-backed peace talks between the countries. 

“We need the American position to be American position. We don’t need signals,” he said.

Zelensky pushed for the U.S. to put “pressure on the situation” especially as he believed “Russia is the aggressor, so that’s why they have to do it.”

“It’s not about comfortable talks. It’s about strong country who can pressure because this country has power and respect,” he concluded. 

The Ukrainian president has previously called for the U.S. and European partners to provide Patriot missile interceptors, which he stated are paramount to shooting down Russian missiles and drones targeting the country’s cities.

Recent Russian strikes hit an apartment building north of Kyiv on Sunday. The attacks killed at least four people and left up to a dozen more buried in the rubble.

U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, said the talks are “making progress” toward ending the conflict, but some challenges still remain. One challenge Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have faced is struggling to include European partners in peace talks.

data.title: Trump: Iran war will be over 'sort of whenever I want it to be'
data.description:
President Trump said the Iran war would be over “sort of whenever I want it to be” as the conflict nears its ninth month and pushback against it grows. 

The president called soldiers at Mar-a-Lago on Thursday alongside first lady Melania Trump, saying they “joined millions of Americans this holiday to pray for your safety and success, and you continue.”

“You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” he stated. “It’s going to be whenever, sort of, whenever I want it to be, to be honest.”

“We’re trying to be nice…we’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives,” he continued. “But I’m not sure if they are going to take advantage of that. Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are.” 

As Democrats prepare to take the majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump faces increasing pressure to end the conflict with Iran. Senate Republicans defeated a resolution earlier this month that would have directed Trump to end hostilities in the Middle East.

In the past month, Iran and the U.S. have engaged in tit-for-tat attacks as both countries face pressure domestically to end the conflict. Iranian strikes targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait, while American forces struck Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz following an unofficial quiet period of roughly two months. 

Two oil tankers were also struck by naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said in a statement, according to state media. The Guard navy accused the tankers of trying to use a route that avoided Iranian control of the strait. 

The conflict’s cost reportedly rose to just more than $47 billion in October, though recently Arthur Miller, the deputy comptroller for budget and appropriations affairs at the Pentagon, told Senators on the Senate Armed Services Committee hearing that the updated cost of the Iran war was $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13.

data.title: Trump signals further openness to working with Democrats on healthcare
data.description:
President Trump signaled an increased openness to working with Democrats on healthcare after the party’s sweeping victories in the midterms, taking control of the House and Senate.

“I have a feeling we’re going to end up with a very bipartisan relationship with the Democrats,” Trump told reporters while at Mar-a-Lago.

“I hope so, where we can take care of a lot of different things, healthcare and so many other things, and get them done,” the president stated.

Trump said Democrats were reaching out to avoid his veto power, which the president signaled he didn’t want to use.

“It’s a very strong power. You have the power of veto, the power of pardon. They’re very, very strong,” he expressed. “They say in many ways they’re the most powerful thing a president has, and I’m not looking to veto everything for two years, and that’s not what they want either.”

“I have a feeling we’re going to have a great relationship, and a lot of things are going to get done,” he concluded. “Maybe more than would have gotten done the more traditional way. It’s happened before.”

While Trump floated working with Democrats on healthcare, he later followed up, saying he was going to “veto, veto, veto until we get legislation that’s going to be great for everybody.”

Expanding healthcare coverage became a campaign promise for many incoming lawmakers, particularly Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.). The incoming senator advocated for a single-payer healthcare bill — commonly referred to as Medicare for All — that he said he would rebrand to “Trumpcare,” in order to garner the president’s support. 

Trump re-shared to Truth Social a social media post El-Sayed made earlier this month, featuring photos of gold-plated “TrumpCare” cards.

El-Sayed on Sunday told NBC News’s Kristen Welker that he didn’t care what it was called, as his “job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country healthcare.”

“Now, I don’t really care what it’s called. I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country,” he stated during his “Meet the Press” interview.

Trump announced the pair are expected to meet regarding El-Sayed’s “Medicare for All” plan, though it is unclear when the meeting is scheduled. 

Trump has been able to work with Democrats on certain COVID-funding packages during his first term, when Republicans only controlled the Senate.
